title: ARCHITECTURAL DESIGN CHARACTERISTICS, USES, AND PERCEPTIONS OF COMMUNITY SPACES IN PERMANENT SUPPORTIVE HOUSING
research_focus: To understand how specific interior spaces in permanent supportive housing, key to the recovery process for single male and female adults recovering from homelessness, might be improved. Specifically, the study examines the therapeutic role of community gathering spaces, their importance to residents, their role in formal and informal social gatherings, and the sociospatial and design factors affecting their desirability and use.

sample_context.description: 38 respondents (26 residents, 12 staff) from two permanent supportive housing locations. Residents were single male and female adults recovering from homelessness, with varying histories of substance abuse, mental difficulties, depression, and trauma. Booth Centre residents were typically 20% female and 80% male; Westgate residents were around 35% female and 65% male. Participants were recruited through posted fliers and email communication.
sample_context.setting: Two permanent supportive housing facilities: Booth Centre (Southampton, UK) and Westgate Community (Tallahassee, Florida, USA). Both are low-barrier, transitional housing programs occupying existing (modified) buildings.

findings.consequent: socialization and formation of meaningful connections
findings.source: Results: Importance of Having Community Spaces and a Sense of Community
findings.theme_name: Importance of having community spaces and a sense of community
findings.description: Staff and a significant majority of residents perceived community spaces as very important for supporting social development, fostering acquaintances and friends, and helping residents feel valued and less isolated, which is crucial for recovery from homelessness.
supporting_quotes: it is good to have acquaintances and friends you can trust. It is starting to help me open up because I'm shy and step out of my comfort zone.
being able to socialize 'is a human rights issue.'

findings.source: Results: Community Spaces Are Underused While Serving as Social Spaces for Many Activities
findings.description: Despite perceived importance, community spaces in both locations are largely underused, typically by only one or two persons at a time, mainly for watching TV. Psychological states (trauma, stress, introversion, depression) and perceived antisocial behaviors by other residents may contribute to this underuse.
supporting_quotes: if they see someone in the room, they will probably not go in.

findings.antecedent: deeper location in building|difficulty of visual and physical access
findings.source: Summary of Findings: Spatial Factors - Location
findings.description: Community spaces located deeper in the building and difficult to find or access visually and physically are less likely to be used. Westgate's front-located spaces were more accessible than Booth Centre's furthest-point spaces, which were perceived as confusing to navigate.
supporting_quotes: there's all these doors and it's not very signposted.

findings.antecedent: visibility into and from space|ability to assess occupancy from a safe distance
findings.consequent: comfort in making space use decisions|likelihood of space use
findings.source: Summary of Findings: Spatial Factors - Visual Access
findings.description: Residents feel more comfortable using community spaces when they can see and assess who is in the space from a safe distance. Lack of visibility creates vulnerability and disincentivizes entry, especially for those with trauma or social anxiety.
supporting_quotes: Knowing that one would need to make a 'prospect and refuge' decision on the spot may lead residents to avoid approaching the space.

findings.antecedent: functional zones (e.g., TV, quiet, game, meeting) separated by wider pathways, low partitions, plants, or furniture with higher backs
findings.consequent: sense of privacy|increased use of community spaces
findings.source: Summary of Findings: Spatial Factors - Functional Zoning
findings.description: Participants suggested that community spaces should be large enough to accommodate different activities through functional zoning, which could create a sense of privacy in each area and encourage greater use.

findings.antecedent: adjacency of community spaces to kitchens
findings.source: Summary of Findings: Spatial Factors - Smaller Kitchens
findings.description: Residents did not find the adjacency of community spaces to kitchens important. Cooking and eating were viewed as separate functions, with residents preferring to eat in the privacy of their own rooms, and many lacking cooking skills or habit of cooking.

findings.antecedent: hominess (cleanliness, acoustics, lighting, personalization)|actual and perceived cleanliness
findings.consequent: sense of dignity and self-esteem|personal stake/care about the place|overall hominess
findings.source: Summary of Findings: Aesthetic Factors - Hominess
findings.description: Hominess, particularly cleanliness, is crucial for dignity and self-esteem among formerly homeless individuals, and indicates a sense of personal stake in the environment. Lack of cleanliness perpetuates feelings of inferiority and dysfunctionality.
supporting_quotes: [I say] Look, we should start being independent and learn how to clean up. Because before we come here a lot of us may not even had a place that we had to take care of.

findings.antecedent: noise from loud conversations and TV
findings.consequent: issue for residents whose rooms were adjacent to community spaces|overall positive assessment of community space
findings.source: Summary of Findings: Aesthetic Factors - Acoustics and daylight
findings.description: Noise from loud conversations and TV was an issue for Booth Centre residents whose rooms were adjacent to the community spaces. In contrast, Westgate's lack of shared partitions contributed to a more positive assessment of its community space.

findings.consequent: pleasantness|feelings of home|importance in community spaces
findings.source: Summary of Findings: Aesthetic Factors - Acoustics and daylight
findings.description: Daylight and views were important features. Residents desired larger windows for more natural light and associated blinds with feelings of home, aligning with biophilic tendencies.
supporting_quotes: One Westgate resident noted how pleasant it was to have blinds on the windows, associating that with feelings of home.

findings.antecedent: unique art, decorative objects, clocks, furnishings (bookshelves, coffee tables, table lighting)|scarcity of furnishings
findings.consequent: emotional investment|sense of ownership|visual enrichment|domestic feeling|institutional feeling|use of space
findings.source: Summary of Findings: Aesthetic Factors - Personalization
findings.description: Personalization and varied furnishings contribute to emotional investment, ownership, and a domestic feeling. Scarcity of furnishings leads to an overpoweringly institutional feeling and reduces space use.
supporting_quotes: Art was mentioned several times as something that residents and staff would like to see more of.

One resident described the cluster lounges as 'dead,' stating that 'it needed more life into it and more stuff: a pool table and a TV and Xbox would help...we need to get art in there or Ping-Pong or something...' concluding that, if that were the case, 'a lot of people wouldn't sit in their [bed]rooms.'

findings.antecedent: policy of restricting access to residents not residing in a cluster/house|security and safety reasons
findings.consequent: residents feeling restricted in recreational and socialization choices|development of relationships|bullying, unproductive, or coercive relationships
findings.source: Summary of Findings: Institutional Policy and Social Factors - Restricting Access Impedes Socializing
findings.theme_name: Institutional Policy: Restricting Access Impedes Socializing
findings.description: Policies restricting access to community spaces, while intended for security, make residents feel restricted and hinder relationship development. Opening up visual access might help but could also exacerbate negative social dynamics.
supporting_quotes: Four Booth Centre residents shared that the cluster system is unnecessarily restrictive and prohibits them from developing relationships as one has to phone people in the same building before vis-iting them.

findings.consequent: psychological belonging, self-esteem, self-fulfillment|perception of caring gesture
findings.source: Summary of Findings: Institutional Policy and Social Factors - Organized Events
findings.description: Participants desired more organized social events, which are important for psychological needs beyond necessities and are perceived as a caring gesture by residents.

derived_hypotheses: An in-depth investigation of how persons perceive socialization would be helpful, including how they would respond to different spatial layout scenarios generally and including access to community rooms.
A second study might examine how real or perceived social behaviors affect community spaces used by residents, affording a look at the effects of bullying and antisocial tendencies.

A third interesting topic that emerged from this study was the use of community kitchens. Data indicated that very few residents used kitchens to prepare or even warm up food, even though cooking ability is closely associated with the idea of being able to take care of oneself and a home in general. Further investigation could also explore connections of architectural design and layouts and their intersections with apparent and implied policies and social hierarchical factors, including in that analysis more buildings with different spatial layouts, increasing sample sizes, and expanding upon the data gathering methods to include statistical behavioral research tools applicable to larger participant sets.
mechanism_candidates: Psychological states of residents (trauma, stress, introversion, depression, mental health conditions) may preclude seeking out opportunities for socializing.
Real or perceived antisocial (aggressive, unwelcoming, bullying) behaviors by other residents may influence community space use.
transferability_limits: The questionnaire sample size presents a limitation for generalizing the findings derived from its data alone.

The study did not address any background characteristics of the respondents, such as personal histories, relationships, health, or where they were in the process of exiting homelessness with regard to residents or the hierarchy of organization, experience with working with homeless persons, or position (i.e. case worker or management) with regard to staff.

Participants may have believed the facility administration was aware of their participation, potentially affecting their responses (e.g., prompting more complimentary answers about facilities' designs and policies).
Some resident participants spoke in dry, institutionalized language of personal responsibility and asserted gratitude, which may have influenced responses.
limitations: The questionnaire sample size presents a limitation for generalizing the findings derived from its data alone.

The study did not address any background characteristics of the respondents, such as personal histories, relationships, health, or where they were in the process of exiting homelessness with regard to residents or the hierarchy of organization, experience with working with homeless persons, or position (i.e. case worker or management) with regard to staff.

Accessing and working directly with persons who had experienced homelessness was a challenge, and participants may have believed the facility administration was aware of their participation, potentially affecting their responses (i.e., prompting more complimentary answers about the facilities' designs and policies).
A number of resident participants spoke in dry, institutionalized language of personal responsibility and asserted that they were grateful for even being in this facility.

paper_metadata.title: Architectural Design Characteristics, Uses, and Perceptions of Community Spaces in Permanent Supportive Housing
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Architectural Design Characteristics, Uses, and Perceptions of Community Spaces in Permanent Supportive Housing
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: People experiencing homelessness often face recoveries complicated by mental disability, substance abuse, and trauma. They can withdraw into self–imposed isolation and avoid important support services, making recovery more difficult. Affirmative relationships developed in part within the designed settings of transitional housing may play a significant role in countering these tendencies. The presence and effectiveness of communal gathering spaces in supportive housing must be better understood as a design problem, particularly given users’ diverse ages, ethnicities, and health needs, which effectively inclusive environments must accommodate. In recent decades, architecture as a discipline has pivoted toward more human–centered approaches, with the individual's dignity and well–being at center stage. This study applies social science–based research methods and spatial analytics to the end of understanding how specific interior spaces, key to the recovery process, might be improved. The authors posit that the success of resident gathering spaces intended to prompt and support resident relationships and decrease users’ feelings of marginalization may be influenced by a range of sociospatial design factors (i.e. visibility and ease of access, adjacencies, access to daylight and views, furniture types, and aesthetics) together with facility policies and events programming. The authors use a combination of space syntax, surveys, and qualitative methods to analyze two contrasting layouts in supportive housing locations in the UK and Florida, drawing conclusions intended to steer the development of typologies for similar facilities.
